q: The IUPAC name of the ester CH₃COOCH₃ is:
x: CH₃COO– comes from ethanoic acid (ethanoate) and –CH₃ from methanol (methyl), so the ester is methyl ethanoate. Ethyl methanoate would be HCOOC₂H₅.

q: The carbon atom of a carboxyl group (–COOH) is:
o: sp³ hybridised with a tetrahedral arrangement
sp² hybridised with a planar arrangement
sp hybridised with a linear arrangement
x: The carboxyl carbon forms three σ bonds and one π bond (to C=O oxygen), so it is sp² hybridised and the group is planar with angles of about 120°.

q: Two molecules of glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH (Mr = 75), join to form the dipeptide glycylglycine. Its relative molecular mass is (H₂O = 18):
x: Forming one peptide bond removes one water molecule: 2 × 75 − 18 = 132. 150 ignores the water lost, and 114 subtracts water twice.

q: Many simple esters, such as those found in fruits, are best known for their:
x: Low-molecular-mass esters are volatile liquids with pleasant fruity smells; they give many fruits and flowers their odours and are used as flavourings.

q: Ethanoic acid (Mr 60) boils at 118 °C, while propan-1-ol (Mr 60) boils at 97 °C. The main reason is that ethanoic acid:
o: Has a much higher molar mass
x: Two ethanoic acid molecules join by two hydrogen bonds to form a dimer, effectively doubling the particle size and the attractions. Both compounds have the same Mr and both hydrogen bond, but the alcohol forms only single hydrogen bonds.

q: Essential amino acids are those that:
o: The body cannot make in sufficient amounts, so they must be obtained from food
Are found only in plant proteins
Contain sulphur in their side chain
x: The body can make some amino acids itself, but essential amino acids must come from dietary protein. A diet lacking any one of them limits the body's protein synthesis.

q: Ethanoic acid reacts with ammonia to form a salt. When this salt is heated strongly, the organic product is:
x: CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COONH₄ (ammonium ethanoate); on heating it loses water: CH₃COONH₄ → CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O, giving ethanamide.

q: Ethanoic acid can be prepared by heating ethanol under reflux with:
x: Acidified dichromate oxidises a primary alcohol first to the aldehyde and, under reflux, on to the carboxylic acid. Concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C dehydrates ethanol to ethene, and LiAlH₄ is a reducing agent.

q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with sodium ethanoate. The organic product is:
x: CH₃COCl + CH₃COONa → (CH₃CO)₂O + NaCl. Two acyl groups joined through an oxygen atom form the acid anhydride.

q: Heating ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, with dilute acid (acid hydrolysis) gives:
x: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + H⁺ → CH₃COOH + NH₄⁺. The –CN carbon becomes the –COOH carbon, so no carbon is lost or gained. Ethanamine forms by reduction of the nitrile, not hydrolysis.

q: Which is the correct order of decreasing reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophiles such as water?
o: Ester > amide > acyl chloride > acid anhydride
Acid anhydride > acyl chloride > ester > amide
Acyl chloride > acid anhydride > ester > amide
Amide > ester > acid anhydride > acyl chloride
x: Cl⁻ is the best leaving group, so acyl chlorides react fastest; anhydrides are next, then esters. Amides are least reactive because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the C=O group.

q: Bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, is heated with ethanolic KCN and the product is then hydrolysed with dilute acid. The final organic product is:
x: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN, which adds one carbon; hydrolysis gives CH₃CH₂COOH, propanoic acid. Propan-1-amine would need reduction of the nitrile instead of hydrolysis.

q: Ethanoyl chloride gives white fumes in moist air because it:
o: Is oxidised by oxygen in the air
Hydrolyses rapidly to ethanoic acid and HCl
Reacts with nitrogen in the air
x: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl. The HCl gas formed meets moisture and produces steamy white fumes.

q: Methylmagnesium bromide, CH₃MgBr, reacts with carbon dioxide and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The organic product is:
x: The Grignard reagent adds to CO₂ to give CH₃COOMgBr, which on acid hydrolysis gives CH₃COOH. CO₂ supplies the extra carboxyl carbon, so the acid has one more carbon than the Grignard reagent.

q: Ethanamide is formed rapidly at room temperature when ammonia reacts with:
x: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl. Chloroethane with ammonia gives an amine (ethylamine), not an amide, and ethanol and ethanal do not give amides.

q: Which reagent gives effervescence of CO₂ with ethanoic acid but no reaction with ethanol?
x: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃; alcohols are not. Sodium and PCl₅ react with both compounds, and acidified dichromate oxidises ethanol.

q: Ethyl ethanoate is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The products are:
x: Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) goes to completion: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH. The acid appears as its sodium salt because NaOH is present.

q: Which is the correct order of decreasing acid strength?
x: Each chlorine withdraws electrons (–I effect), spreading the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilising it, so more chlorines mean a stronger acid. Thinking that chlorine 'adds bulk' and weakens the acid gives the reversed order.

q: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. The reason is that:
o: Methanoic acid has a larger molar mass
The methyl group withdraws electrons from the carboxyl group
Methanoic acid has two oxygen atoms and ethanoic acid only one
The methyl group in ethanoic acid donates electrons, destabilising the ethanoate ion
x: –CH₃ has a +I (electron-releasing) effect, which increases the negative charge on the carboxylate oxygens and makes ethanoate less stable, so ethanoic acid ionises less. Both acids contain two oxygens, and methanoic acid is the lighter one, so those options are factually wrong.

q: 6.0 g of ethanoic acid reacts completely with excess sodium hydrogencarbonate. What volume of CO₂ is given off at STP? (CH₃COOH = 60 g mol⁻¹, molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂, a 1 : 1 ratio. 6.0 ÷ 60 = 0.1 mol, giving 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³. Using the 2 : 1 ratio of the carbonate (Na₂CO₃) reaction gives 1.12 dm³.

q: Ethanoic acid is reduced with lithium aluminium hydride, LiAlH₄, in dry ether, followed by dilute acid. The organic product is:
x: LiAlH₄ is strong enough to reduce –COOH right down to –CH₂OH, giving CH₃CH₂OH; the aldehyde is only an intermediate and is not isolated. Stopping at ethanal is the tempting slip; the carbon chain is not shortened.

q: Which is the correct order of decreasing acidity?
x: The ethanoate ion is stabilised by two equivalent oxygens and phenoxide by delocalisation into the ring, so ethanoic acid > phenol (only ethanoic acid releases CO₂ from NaHCO₃). The ethyl group's +I effect makes ethanol slightly weaker than water. Putting ethanol above water forgets this +I effect.

q: Ethanoic acid is esterified with ethanol whose oxygen is the isotope ¹⁸O, using concentrated H₂SO₄. After reaction the ¹⁸O is found in:
o: Both ethyl ethanoate and water equally
x: In acid-catalysed esterification the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to the ethyl group, while the –OH of the acid leaves as water. So the label ends up in CH₃CO–¹⁸O–C₂H₅. Assuming the alcohol loses its –OH (as in alcohol + HX) puts the label in water, the tempting slip.

q: For CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, Kc = 4 at the reaction temperature. Starting with 1 mol of each reactant, how many moles of ester are present at equilibrium?
x: If x mol ester forms: x² / (1 − x)² = 4, so x / (1 − x) = 2 and x = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 mol. Forgetting to take the square root, x / (1 − x) = 4, gives 0.80 mol.

q: Compared with ethanoic acid, ethanoyl chloride is a better reagent for making ethyl ethanoate from ethanol. The reason is that ethanoyl chloride:
o: Gives water as by-product, which drives the reaction forward
Needs concentrated H₂SO₄ as a catalyst
Gives an equilibrium mixture with a higher Kc
Reacts quickly at room temperature and goes to completion, giving HCl as by-product
x: CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl is fast and essentially one-way because Cl⁻ is a good leaving group and HCl escapes. The acid route gives water, is reversible, and needs H₂SO₄ and heating, which are the features the distractors wrongly give to the acyl chloride.

q: Ethanoic acid is heated with phosphorus pentoxide, P₂O₅, a strong dehydrating agent. The organic product is:
x: P₂O₅ removes one H₂O from two acid molecules: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O. Ethanoyl chloride would need PCl₅, PCl₃ or SOCl₂, the tempting mix-up of phosphorus reagents.

q: In the solid state and in neutral water, glycine exists mainly as the zwitterion:
x: The acidic –COOH group gives its proton to the basic –NH₂ group in the same molecule, giving a dipolar ion with both charges and no net charge. ⁺H₃NCH₂COOH is the form in strong acid and H₂NCH₂COO⁻ the form in strong base.

q: Glycine is dissolved in dilute hydrochloric acid (pH about 1). The main form present is:
x: Excess H⁺ protonates the –COO⁻ of the zwitterion, so the species is the cation ⁺H₃NCH₂COOH with a net charge of +1. Leaving the zwitterion unchanged ignores the acid; H₂NCH₂COO⁻ is the form in strong base.

q: Glycine is dissolved in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. The main glycine species is:
x: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from the –NH₃⁺ group of the zwitterion, leaving the anion H₂NCH₂COO⁻ (net charge −1). Removing a proton from the ammonium end, not adding one, is the key step; picking the cation reverses acid and base.

q: Amino acids such as glycine are crystalline solids with high melting points (glycine decomposes above 230 °C), unlike most organic compounds of similar Mr. The main reason is that:
o: They form only weak London forces
They exist as zwitterions, held together by strong ionic attractions
x: The ⁺H₃N– and –COO⁻ ends of neighbouring zwitterions attract strongly, as in an ionic lattice, so much energy is needed to melt them; the same charges make them soluble in water. Glycine (Mr 75) is a small molecule with no ring, so size or a ring cannot explain it.

q: How many peptide (–CO–NH–) bonds are present in a pentapeptide, a chain made of five amino acid units?
x: Each peptide bond joins two neighbouring units, so a chain of n units has n − 1 peptide bonds: 5 − 1 = 4. Counting one bond per amino acid gives the tempting 5.

q: How many different dipeptides can be formed from glycine and alanine, if each amino acid may be used once or twice?
x: The two ends of a dipeptide are different (free –NH₂ end and free –COOH end), so Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly are different compounds; with Gly-Gly and Ala-Ala that makes 4. Treating Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly as the same gives the tempting 3.

q: Which amino acid has no chiral (asymmetric) carbon atom and so is not optically active?
x: The α-carbon of glycine carries two hydrogen atoms, so it does not have four different groups. In alanine, serine and valine the α-carbon carries H, NH₂, COOH and a different side chain, so each is chiral.

q: In electrophoresis, an amino acid in a buffer at its isoelectric point (pI):
o: Moves towards the cathode, because it carries an –NH₃⁺ group
Does not move, because its net charge is zero
Moves towards the anode, because it carries a –COO⁻ group
Splits into two spots that move in opposite directions
x: At the isoelectric point the amino acid is present as the zwitterion, whose positive and negative charges cancel, so the electric field gives no net pull. Below the pI it is a cation and moves to the cathode; above it an anion moving to the anode.

q: A drop of glycine solution is placed in the middle of an electrophoresis strip soaked in a buffer of pH 1, and a voltage is applied. The glycine:
o: Splits into two spots moving in opposite directions
x: At pH 1, far below the isoelectric point of glycine (about 6), the zwitterion is protonated to ⁺H₃NCH₂COOH, a cation, which is attracted to the negative electrode. Remembering that the cathode is negative is the key step; picking the anode mixes up the electrodes.
